units.translation: ⟦1⟧.: so Athene 699 ⟦2⟧; but in detail Plato Laws III, 693 D—699 D, where by the examples of the Persians and Athenians, in older and in more recent times, it is shown how moderate kingship and freedom not lacking in fear are beneficial, whereas unlimited despotism and unbridled freedom are ruinous. With the Eumenides, however, there is no contact, since the Areopagus is not mentioned. (Cf. Introduction p. 13). - ⟦3⟧ (Wieseler; cf. f g h) relates to ⟦4⟧ (M) as ⟦5⟧ (⟦6⟧. 624) to ⟦7⟧; but while this occurs in A. (⟦8⟧, ⟦9⟧), he does not have ⟦10⟧, but instead (699) ⟦11⟧, so that the correction is justified and here too (as at 492) the exact responsion is to be established. (⟦12⟧ ⟦13⟧.) ⟦14⟧ (aorist) refers to the individual case. For the saying about the right mean one compares again Plato, ⟦15⟧ X, 619 A ⟦16⟧; but also already ⟦17⟧ ⟦18⟧· ⟦19⟧, ⟦20⟧ ⟦21⟧, ⟦22⟧. Then Euripides Frg. 80 N. ⟦23⟧ etc. ⟦24⟧’ ⟦25⟧̄ ⟦26⟧ (⟦27⟧, ⟦28⟧. 676) can be understood as "the one so, the other otherwise", like ⟦29⟧ etc.; however also (Paley) that which is different from the ⟦30⟧ in correspondingly different manner. The first explanation, however, lies closer, and contains more: first, that the deity oversees and directs everything, and then, that it treats different things differently, as is set out in the following verses.
I advise the citizens to honor neither anarchy nor despotism
always to choose the middle life among such things and to flee the extremes in either direction
the middle is best in all things
for I find that the middle things in a city flourish with longer prosperity
I blame the fate of tyrannies
for mortals, things greater than the middle breed diseases
one from one place, another from another

⟦1⟧ cannot mean the same as ⟦2⟧, as the scholiast explains, but must (like ⟦3⟧) have the meaning "corresponding", namely to the difference of mental dispositions and their consequences. The impious disposition produces wantonness and the deeds arising from wantonness and the consequences of these deeds; on the other hand, with health of mind all blessing is connected as its consequence, as both are further shown in Antistr. ⟦4⟧, Str. Ant. ⟦5⟧. ⟦6⟧ forms the opposite to ⟦7⟧ ⟦8⟧ of Xerxes' arrogance, who believed himself superior to all the gods;
⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ (the latter Sophocles) the tragedians use according to the rhythm.
